content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects approximately 1.7% of the population. A significant proportion of individuals with ASD experience language difficulties, with 25% to 30% of children with ASD either failing to develop functional language or remaining minimally verbal. Effective communication is a critical life skill, and deficits in this area can lead to negative outcomes such as lower academic performance, behavioral challenges, and diminished quality of life. Historically, research on communication interventions for ASD has primarily focused on verbal children, and it cannot be assumed that these interventions are equally effective for minimally verbal children with ASD. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of communication interventions specifically designed for minimally verbal children with ASD. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children under 12 years of age who were minimally verbal, defined as having fewer than 30 functional words or being unable to use speech alone to communicate. The interventions were compared to no treatment, wait-list control, or treatment as usual. The search for relevant studies was conducted in November 2017 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, as well as 12 additional databases and three trial registries. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were also examined, and experts in the field were contacted to identify ongoing or unpublished studies. Two RCTs met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 154 children aged 32 months to 11 years. One study evaluated a verbally based intervention called Focused Playtime Intervention (FPI), while the other assessed an alternative and augmentative communication (AAC) intervention known as the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS). The FPI study was conducted in the United States and included 70 minimally verbal children with ASD, aged 32 to 82 months. This intervention aimed to enhance coordinated toy play between the child and parent. Parents received 12 in-home training sessions, each lasting 90 minutes, over a 12-week period. Additionally, they were invited to attend parent advocacy coaching sessions. The study was funded by the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, the MIND Institute Research Program, and a Professional Staff Congress-City University of New York grant. The PECS study was conducted in the United Kingdom and involved 84 minimally verbal children with ASD, aged 4 to 11 years. These children were not using PECS beyond phase 1 at baseline and attended autism-specific classes with a typical child-to-adult ratio of 2:1. Teachers and parents participated in a two-day PECS training workshop, and PECS consultants provided six half-day consultations to each class over a five-month period. This study was funded by the Three Guineas Trust. Both studies were assessed as having a high or unclear risk of bias in at least four of the seven Risk of bias categories, with the lack of blinding for participants and personnel being a significant concern. Using the GRADE approach, the overall quality of evidence was rated as very low due to issues such as risk of bias, small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, and the fact that only one trial was available for each type of intervention (verbally based or AAC). The primary focus of both studies was on communication outcomes, including verbal and non-verbal communication. The FPI study did not find significant improvements in spoken communication, as measured by the expressive language domain of the Mullen Scale of Early Learning, immediately after the intervention. However, children with lower baseline expressive language (less than 11.3 months age-equivalent) showed greater improvement compared to those with higher baseline expressive language. Some children did achieve expressive language gains as a result of the intervention. The PECS study found that children in the AAC intervention group were significantly more likely to use verbal initiations and PECS symbols immediately after the intervention. However, these gains were not sustained 10 months later. There was no evidence that the AAC intervention improved the frequency of speech, verbal expressive vocabulary, social communication, or pragmatic language immediately post-intervention. Neither intervention (FPI or PECS) resulted in sustained improvements in spoken or non-verbal communication for most children. Additionally, neither study collected data on adverse events, other communication skills, quality of life, or behavioral outcomes. In conclusion, there is limited evidence to support the effectiveness of verbally based and AAC interventions in improving spoken and non-verbal communication in minimally verbal children with ASD. While the AAC intervention demonstrated short-term gains in PECS use and verbal/non-verbal initiations, these improvements were not maintained over time. The verbally based intervention did not result in significant gains in expressive language overall, although children with lower baseline expressive language showed more improvement. Future RCTs should compare different interventions, include control groups, and investigate additional outcomes such as adverse events, quality of life, and behavioral changes. This would provide a better understanding of treatment effects and allow for the exploration of factors that may influence intervention outcomes.
